def: A setup that sends each request to a cheap model first and escalates to a larger one only when a check says the cheap answer is not good enough.
The set of options that no other option beats on every axis at once; when choosing a model you only consider those on the frontier of quality, cost and latency.
A component that reads a request before any model call and picks which model should answer it, usually from a predicted-difficulty score and a threshold.
The fraction of requests or time that a service works, often quoted in nines: 99.9% allows about 43.2 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month.
When two supposedly independent components tend to fail together because of a shared cause, which makes a fallback far less protective than the independent calculation suggests.
Sending a second copy of a slow request after a short delay and using whichever answer returns first, trading a little extra load for a much shorter tail latency.
A guard that stops calling a failing dependency after the error rate passes a threshold, failing fast or using a fallback, then probes carefully to see if it has recovered.
Designing a ladder of worse-but-working modes (fallback model, cache, non-LLM path, honest error) so that a failure reduces quality instead of stopping the feature.
A rate limiter with a capacity b and a refill rate r: each request spends permits, so at most b + rT requests are admitted in any window of length T.
A tenant whose heavy usage consumes shared capacity and degrades service for others, prevented with per-tenant quotas.
An allocation rule that gives everyone an equal share, lets those who need less take only what they need, and redistributes the surplus among those who want more.
How fast a budget is being consumed relative to plan: observed spend or error rate divided by the allowed rate, where 1 means exactly on track.
The amount of failure an SLO allows over a period, for example 43.2 minutes a month at 99.9%, used to decide whether to ship changes or fix reliability.
The latency below which a given share of requests fall, for example p95 is the value that 95% of requests beat; it describes the slow tail that averages hide.
The chain of steps in a request that determines its total time when some steps run in parallel; speeding up anything off it changes nothing.
A blameless written review of an incident with impact, timeline, causes and owned action items, aimed at fixing the system rather than blaming people.
Copying real requests to a candidate version and discarding its output so that cost, latency and answer differences can be measured with no user impact.
Serving a new version to a small share of real traffic first; with failure rate p, n canary requests catch it with probability 1 - (1 - p)^n.

Replacing personal data in text with typed placeholders before it is logged or sent onward; because recall is never perfect, some leakage remains and must be contained by access control and retention.
Refusing or degrading when a safety check cannot run, instead of proceeding without it; the right choice when a missed harm costs far more than a blocked good request.
